coach_says: You traded off your dark-squared bishop on d2, so g7 has no natural defender. Taking back with the queen offers a queen trade, but White simply declines with Qg4, hitting g7 and the h8 rook, and you have to play Kf8 and give up castling. Recapturing with the pawn (exd5) keeps your queen out of the way and keeps the position closed. After trading a fianchetto-side or dark-squared bishop, check whether the enemy queen can reach g4 or g5 and hit g7.

Qb3 lines up on b5, but it puts your queen where Black's pawns can kick it: ...c4 hits b3 with tempo, and the pawn is protected by d5, so you can't take it with the queen. You lose time retreating, Black's queenside pawns gain space, and your d3 pawn and king in the centre become targets (ideas like ...Ne5 and ...Nd3+). Before putting your queen on a square, check whether an enemy pawn can attack it next move. Here castling first (O-O) was the calm, safe choice.

Bg4 attacks the queen, but the queen just moves to a better square: Qb3 now threatens both Qxb7 and Bf7+ followed by Bxg6, because your f-pawn has gone and the light squares around your king are weak. Your bishop also left c8, where it was guarding b7 and e6, and f3 will kick it later anyway. Before chasing a queen, ask where it will go and what it will hit from there; here a developing move like Nc6 was better.
concept: chasing the queen to a better square
also: weak light squares f7 and e6

coach_says: Black's bishop on d7 was attacking your a4 pawn, and nothing defended it. Ng4 ignores that, so Black takes on a4, wins a pawn and opens lines towards your king on c1, with the a-pawn free to run down the board. b3 would have protected a4 and kept your queenside pawns solid. Before starting your own kingside plans, ask what your opponent's last move threatened.
